chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Hamza ibn Humran, from his father, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when it is His will to honor a servant who has a sin, He tests him with sickness. If He does not do that for him, He tests him with need (poverty). If He does not do that with him, He makes death difficult for him to compensate for that sin with it.

He (peace be upon him) said: And when it is His will to humble a servant who has a good deed with Him, He grants health to his body. If He does not do that with him, He expands his sustenance for him. If he does not do that with him, He eases death for him to compensate for that good deed with it.
ai.seo_question: What is the wisdom behind illness, poverty, and death in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the concept of *tadhyil* (hastening recompense), where God uses worldly afflictions or blessings to settle a servant's spiritual account before the Hereafter. Specifically, it highlights the paradox that trials like sickness or poverty may be signs of divine honor for a sinner, while ease and health may serve to humble a righteous person, ensuring their good deeds are fully rewarded in this life.
